No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Disentangling Recall and Reasoning in Transformer Models through Layer-wise Attention and Activation Analysis
papers.research_question: Does recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on overlapping or separable internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that recall and reasoning in transformer models rely on partially distinct internal circuits, with early layers supporting recall and deeper layers enabling reasoning, supported by causal evidence from interventions.
papers.conclusion: The Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct model develops a hierarchically organized division between recall and reasoning, with early layers for recall and deeper layers for reasoning, supported by task-specific attention heads and MLP neurons.
papers.key_findings:
Layer specialization: early layers (0–6) predominantly support factual recall, while later layers (17–27) concentrate on reasoning.
Head-level differentiation: 74% of attention heads show significant task preferences, with recall-preferring heads in shallower layers and reasoning-preferring heads in deeper layers.
MLP neuron selectivity: roughly one-third of MLP neurons exhibit task-specific activation patterns, with clusters in layers 4 (recall) and 22 (reasoning).
Selective impairment: disabling recall-associated circuits reduces factual accuracy by up to 15% while leaving reasoning unaffected, and vice versa for reasoning circuits.
Consistency: these specialization patterns are statistically stable across cross-validation and robust to normalization choices.
future_direction: Extend experiments to larger, contemporary models such as LLaMA and Mistral.
Expand the dataset to encompass more diverse reasoning phenomena.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models excel at both recall (retrieving memorized facts) and reasoning (performing multi-step inference), but whether these abilities rely on distinct internal mechanisms remains unclear. Distinguishing recall from reasoning is crucial for predicting model generalization, designing targeted evaluations, and building safer interventions that affect one ability without disrupting the other.We approach this question through mechanistic interpretability, using controlled datasets of synthetic linguistic puzzles to probe transformer models at the layer, head, and neuron level. Our pipeline combines activation patching and structured ablations to causally measure component contributions to each task type. Across two model families (Qwen and LLaMA), we find that interventions on distinct layers and attention heads lead to selective impairments: disabling identified "recall circuits" reduces fact-retrieval accuracy by up to 15\% while leaving reasoning intact, whereas disabling "reasoning circuits" reduces multi-step inference by a comparable margin. At the neuron level, we observe task-specific firing patterns, though these effects are less robust, consistent with neuronal polysemanticity.Our results provide the first causal evidence that recall and reasoning rely on separable but interacting circuits in transformer models. These findings advance mechanistic interpretability by linking circuit-level structure to functional specialization and demonstrate how controlled datasets and causal interventions can yield mechanistic insights into model cognition, informing safer deployment of large language models.

papers.title: Plausibility Processing in Transformer Language Models: Focusing on the Role of Attention Heads in GPT
papers.research_question: How do Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, specifically the plausibility of noun-verb relations, and what is the causal role of attention heads in this processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that GPT2 processes noun-verb plausibility similarly to humans and identifies a set of attention heads that detect plausibility. It shows these heads collectively and causally contribute to the model's plausibility processing, with contributions being imbalanced and not strictly correlated with individual head performance.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that semantic plausibility knowledge in GPT2 is processed by a diffusely distributed set of attention heads that make imbalanced but collective causal contributions, highlighting the importance of causal analysis in understanding attention head functions.
papers.key_findings:
GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer models (BERT, RoBERTa, ALBERT).
GPT2 contains 18 attention heads distributed across layers that are sensitive to noun-verb plausibility, independent of syntactic dependency.
Pruning these plausibility-processing heads eliminates GPT2's plausibility sensitivity, while pruning a random set of heads does not.
The causal contribution of individual plausibility-processing heads to the model's overall ability is imbalanced; a single head (0,10) accounts for a large portion of the effect for syntactic dependents.
The performance of an attention head in detecting plausibility (accuracy) does not necessarily correlate with its causal contribution to the model's overall plausibility processing ability.
papers.limitation:
The scope of the study is restricted to the plausibility of noun-verb relations, not covering other types of semantic knowledge.
The study does not detail how attention heads interact with other components like hidden states across layers or feed-forward networks.
future_direction: Expand the study's scope to a broader array of semantic knowledge for better generalizability.
Investigate interactions between attention heads and other model components (e.g., hidden states, feed-forward networks) to better understand their role in semantic knowledge processing.
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to explore how Transformer language models process semantic knowledge, especially regarding the plausibility of noun-verb relations. First, I demonstrate GPT2 exhibits a higher degree of similarity with humans in plausibility processing compared to other Transformer language models. Next, I delve into how knowledge of plausibility is contained within attention heads of GPT2 and how these heads causally contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability. Through several experiments, it was found that: i) GPT2 has a number of attention heads that detect plausible noun-verb relationships; ii) these heads collectively contribute to the Transformer's ability to process plausibility, albeit to varying degrees; and iii) attention heads' individual performance in detecting plausibility does not necessarily correlate with how much they contribute to GPT2's plausibility processing ability.

papers.title: Factual Self-Awareness in Language Models: Representation, Robustness, and Scaling
papers.research_question: Do language models have an internal compass that dictates the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation? Specifically, are there linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that indicate whether the model will recall a correct attribute?
papers.core_contribution: Language models encode linear features in the residual stream that indicate whether they will correctly recall a factual attribute, and this self-awareness signal is robust to formatting variations and emerges early in training.
papers.conclusion: Language models possess intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities for factual recall, which contributes to their interpretability and reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes and sparse autoencoders (SAEs) show that factual self-awareness is encoded as linear directions in the residual stream, separable between known and forgotten factual associations.
The self-awareness signal is robust to superficial perturbations like quotation marks, but sensitive to structural changes like rephrasing as questions.
The signal emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers.
Larger models (within a family) do not necessarily have more linearly decodable self-awareness representations.
The class balance of known and forgotten samples depends on the sampling parameters (k, l) used to define them.
papers.limitation:
Defining knowledge at the entity level is a limitation: when an LM fabricates factual associations, it may invent attributes for a known entity.
Some input templates introduced spurious correlations due to their phrasing, which had to be excluded.
papers.abstract: Factual incorrectness in generated content is one of the primary concerns in ubiquitous deployment of large language models (LLMs). Prior findings suggest LLMs can (sometimes) detect factual incorrectness in their generated content (i.e., fact-checking post-generation). In this work, we provide evidence supporting the presence of LLMs' internal compass that dictate the correctness of factual recall at the time of generation. We demonstrate that for a given subject entity and a relation, LLMs internally encode linear features in the Transformer's residual stream that dictate whether it will be able to recall the correct attribute (that forms a valid entity-relation-attribute triplet). This self-awareness signal is robust to minor formatting variations. We investigate the effects of context perturbation via different example selection strategies. Scaling experiments across model sizes and training dynamics highlight that self-awareness emerges rapidly during training and peaks in intermediate layers. These findings uncover intrinsic self-monitoring capabilities within LLMs, contributing to their interpretability and reliability.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does this paper investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that large language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their internal states through concept injection experiments.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited but functional introspective awareness, which is unreliable but may improve with model capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Models can detect and identify injected concepts in their activations.
Models can distinguish between injected thoughts and text inputs.
Models can use introspection to detect artificially prefilled outputs.
Models can modulate their internal representations when instructed to think about concepts.
Introspective capabilities are more pronounced in more capable models like Claude Opus 4 and 4.1.
papers.limitation:
The abilities observed are highly unreliable; failures of introspection remain the norm.
Experiments do not pin down specific mechanistic explanations.
Concept injection places models in an unnatural setting.
future_direction: Identifying metacognitive representations more clearly
Investigating the grounding of emotional responses in introspective reports
Exploring introspective capabilities in more natural conditions
papers.abstract: We investigate whether large language models can introspect on their internal states. It is difficult to answer this question through conversation alone, as genuine introspection cannot be distinguished from confabulations. Here, we address this challenge by injecting representations of known concepts into a model's activations, and measuring the influence of these manipulations on the model's self-reported states. We find that models can, in certain scenarios, notice the presence of injected concepts and accurately identify them. Models demonstrate some ability to recall prior internal representations and distinguish them from raw text inputs. Strikingly, we find that some models can use their ability to recall prior intentions in order to distinguish their own outputs from artificial prefills. In all these experiments, Claude Opus 4 and 4.1, the most capable models we tested, generally demonstrate the greatest introspective awareness; however, trends across models are complex and sensitive to post-training strategies. Finally, we explore whether models can explicitly control their internal representations, finding that models can modulate their activations when instructed or incentivized to "think about" a concept. Overall, our results indicate that current language models possess some functional introspective awareness of their own internal states. We stress that in today's models, this capacity is highly unreliable and context-dependent; however, it may continue to develop with further improvements to model capabilities.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Neuron-Level Knowledge Attribution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to identify important neurons for knowledge storage in large language models, and how to distinguish between 'value neurons' that directly contribute to predictions and 'query neurons' that activate them.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a static method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' in LLMs, and a method based on inner products to identify 'query neurons' that activate them, showing superior performance compared to other static methods.
papers.conclusion: The study proposes a method based on log probability increase to identify important 'value neurons' and a method based on inner products to locate the 'query neurons' activating them, which aids in understanding the mechanism of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Both attention and FFN layers can store knowledge, and all important neurons directly contributing to knowledge prediction are in deep layers.
In attention layers, knowledge with similar semantics tends to be stored in the same heads, while distinct semantics are stored in different heads.
Intervening on a few value neurons (300) or query neurons (1000) can significantly influence the final prediction.
FFN value neurons are mainly activated by medium-deep attention value neurons, which are mainly activated by shallow/medium FFN query neurons.
The proposed attribution method outperforms seven other static methods across three metrics.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on six specific types of knowledge, while other types are also important.
Experiments are conducted only on GPT2-large and Llama-7B models; comparison across different models is needed.
Uses static methods for attribution and does not compare with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.
future_direction: Compare static methods with other attribution methods like causal mediation analysis and gradient-based methods.
Explore knowledge storage in other types of knowledge and across different models.
Improve attribution methods to better capture the importance of deepest layers and interpretability of query neurons.
papers.abstract: Identifying important neurons for final predictions is essential for understanding the mechanisms of large language models. Due to computational constraints, current attribution techniques struggle to operate at neuron level. In this paper, we propose a static method for pinpointing significant neurons. Compared to seven other methods, our approach demonstrates superior performance across three metrics. Additionally, since most static methods typically only identify "value neurons" directly contributing to the final prediction, we propose a method for identifying "query neurons" which activate these "value neurons". Finally, we apply our methods to analyze six types of knowledge across both attention and feed-forward network (FFN) layers. Our method and analysis are helpful for understanding the mechanisms of knowledge storage and set the stage for future research in knowledge editing. The code is available on https://github.com/zepingyu0512/neuron-attribution.

papers.title: Are Human Conversations Special? A Large Language Model Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the differences in attention mechanisms of large language models when processing human-human conversations compared to web content, code, and mathematical texts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that human-human conversations pose unique challenges for LLMs, with higher attention dispersion and longer contextual dependencies, indicating a need for more domain-specific training data.
papers.conclusion: The study emphasizes the need for domain-specialized language models for human conversations due to significant differences in attention behaviors and data scarcity.
papers.key_findings:
Human-human conversations exhibit higher attention distance differences in deeper layers compared to web data, indicating longer contextual dependencies.
Attention entropy is higher in human conversations, suggesting more attention dispersion and complexity.
The Interdependency Factor is higher for human conversations, showing more interconnected token relationships.
Human conversations are underrepresented in web data used for pretraining LLMs.
t-SNE visualizations show distinct hidden state representations for human conversations and math compared to web and code in deeper layers.
future_direction: Developing domain-specialized language models for human conversations
Incorporating more diverse and authentic conversational data into training
papers.abstract: This study analyzes changes in the attention mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) when used to understand natural conversations between humans (human-human). We analyze three use cases of LLMs: interactions over web content, code, and mathematical texts. By analyzing attention distance, dispersion, and interdependency across these domains, we highlight the unique challenges posed by conversational data. Notably, conversations require nuanced handling of long-term contextual relationships and exhibit higher complexity through their attention patterns. Our findings reveal that while language models exhibit domain-specific attention behaviors, there is a significant gap in their ability to specialize in human conversations. Through detailed attention entropy analysis and t-SNE visualizations, we demonstrate the need for models trained with a diverse array of high-quality conversational data to enhance understanding and generation of human-like dialogue. This research highlights the importance of domain specialization in language models and suggests pathways for future advancement in modeling human conversational nuances.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: Time Course MechInterp: Analyzing the Evolution of Components and Knowledge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Which components (attention heads, FFNs) contribute to solving factual knowledge tasks, and how do these circuits for factual knowledge evolve over the course of model training?
papers.core_contribution: This work provides a mechanistic view of how factual knowledge representation evolves during LLM pre-training, showing that models initially rely on general-purpose components which later specialize, with attention heads exhibiting high turnover and FFNs remaining more stable.
papers.conclusion: The study offers insights into the hierarchical learning process of LLMs, where general components form first and later diversify, with attention heads being highly adaptive and FFNs providing stable processing.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads show high turnover and dynamic role transitions, while FFNs are more stable throughout training.
Location-based relations (LOC) converge to high accuracy earlier in training than name-based relations (NAME).
LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.
Answer-specific attention heads demonstrate the highest turnover, indicating frequent role changes.
FFNs act as a steady processing backbone, with most remaining in general roles.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints prevented analysis at the neuron level and the use of alternative interpretability techniques like activation patching across all snapshots.
The dataset is limited to English and covers only location-based and name-based factual relations.
The analysis uses a fixed activation threshold for role classification, which may introduce bias.
Only a subset of training snapshots was analyzed, leaving gaps in tracking role transitions.
Direct comparison with other model families (e.g., Pythia) was not feasible due to architectural differences preventing the use of IFRs.
future_direction: Incorporate more diverse datasets, additional model variants, and alternative interpretability techniques.
Expand analysis to other domains, multilingual settings, and ambiguous queries.
Investigate the long-term impact of component dynamics on fine-tuning, pruning, and continual learning.
papers.abstract: Understanding how large language models (LLMs) acquire and store factual knowledge is crucial for enhancing their interpretability and reliability.In this work, we analyze the evolution of factual knowledge representation in the OLMo-7B model by tracking the roles of its attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) over the course of pre-training.We classify these components into four roles: general, entity, relation-answer, and fact-answer specific and examine their stability and transitions.Our results show that LLMs initially depend on broad, general-purpose components, which later specialize as training progresses.Once the model reliably predicts answers, some components are repurposed, suggesting an adaptive learning process.Notably, attention heads display the highest turnover.We also present evidence that FFNs remain more stable throughout training.Furthermore, our probing experiments reveal that location-based relations converge to high accuracy earlier in training than namebased relations, highlighting how task complexity shapes acquisition dynamics.These insights offer a mechanistic view of knowledge formation in LLMs.We release the code and data. 1

papers.title: Computational Basis of LLM's Decision Making in Social Simulation
papers.research_question: How are social meanings internally represented in LLMs, and how can those internal representations be systematically manipulated to steer model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for extracting and manipulating social concept vectors in LLMs' residual streams to steer decision-making in social simulations, specifically demonstrated in a Dictator Game.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a practical bridge between sociological theory and the internal geometry of modern language models, turning LLMs from opaque black boxes into calibrated instruments for theory testing, bounded synthetic data, and auditable interventions.
papers.key_findings:
Social variables like framing (give vs. take) and social distance (stranger meet) significantly affect the LLM's decision to transfer money in the Dictator Game.
These variables are encoded as vectors in the residual stream, and their alignment with the decision vector can be measured via cosine similarity and dot product.
By projecting and injecting these variable vectors into the residual stream, the model's decisions can be steered in a controlled manner.
The steering effect is layer-dependent and can be fine-tuned by adjusting the injection coefficient, with earlier layers having more amplified effects.
The method allows for precise manipulation of specific variables (e.g., gender) without affecting others, enabling targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on internal representational validity and controlled steering within the model's activation space, but does not establish external sociological validity (i.e., correspondence to human cognition and behavior).
The method requires access to the model's internal weights and activations, so it is only feasible with open-weight models.
future_direction: From Scripts to User-Friendly Tools: developing a user-friendly software package to make activation-based steering more accessible.
Expanding to other Social Constructs and Experiments: applying the framework to a wider range of social constructs and experimental paradigms.
Bridging the Gap Between Internal and External Validity: conducting systematic human-LLM comparisons to establish external sociological validity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly serve as human-like decision-making agents in social science and applied settings. These LLM-agents are typically assigned human-like characters and placed in real-life contexts. However, how these characters and contexts shape an LLM's behavior remains underexplored. This study proposes and tests methods for probing, quantifying, and modifying an LLM's internal representations in a Dictator Game, a classic behavioral experiment on fairness and prosocial behavior. We extract ``vectors of variable variations'' (e.g., ``male'' to ``female'') from the LLM's internal state. Manipulating these vectors during the model's inference can substantially alter how those variables relate to the model's decision-making. This approach offers a principled way to study and regulate how social concepts can be encoded and engineered within transformer-based models, with implications for alignment, debiasing, and designing AI agents for social simulations in both academic and commercial applications, strengthening sociological theory and measurement.

papers.title: Associative memory inspires improvements for in-context learning using a novel attention residual stream architecture
papers.research_question: How can insights from associative memory models be used to improve in-context learning (ICL) in Transformer-based language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory, that allows information to flow directly between attention heads, leading to faster and improved in-context learning in Transformers.
papers.conclusion: The residual attention stream architecture, inspired by associative memory models, improves in-context learning in Transformers and shows promising scalability to larger language models.
papers.key_findings:
A one-layer associative memory model (AMICL) can perform in-context learning on a classification task.
Adding a residual stream for attention values (and to a lesser extent, queries) in a two-layer Transformer speeds up the emergence of ICL during training compared to a classic Transformer.
Naively applying the residual value stream architecture to small language models (8M and 1B parameters) trained on Tiny Stories indicates performance improvements scale to larger models and more naturalistic data.
future_direction: Testing the residual attention stream architecture on larger models and more complex tasks.
Exploring the interpretability of the residual stream for understanding model mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate an impressive ability to utilise information within the context of their input sequences to appropriately respond to data unseen by the LLM during its training procedure. This ability is known as in-context learning (ICL). Humans and non-human animals demonstrate similar abilities, however their neural architectures differ substantially from LLMs. Despite this, a critical component within LLMs, the attention mechanism, resembles modern associative memory models, widely used in and influenced by the computational neuroscience community to model biological memory systems. Using this connection, we introduce an associative memory model capable of performing ICL. We use this as inspiration for a novel residual stream architecture which allows information to directly flow between attention heads. We test this architecture during training within a two-layer Transformer and show its ICL abilities manifest more quickly than without this modification. We then apply our architecture in small language models with 8 million and 1 billion parameters, focusing on attention head values, with results also indicating improved performance at these larger and more naturalistic scales.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations. The intervention is dependent upon the ability to reliably extract the model's typical state when correctly solving a task. Our results suggest that reasoning performance can be modulated in the same manner as other information-processing tasks performed by LLMs and demonstrate that we are capable of improving performance on specific tasks via a simple intervention on the residual stream with no additional training.

papers.title: Interpreting Key Mechanisms of Factual Recall in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based language models perform factual recall, specifically how do they extract arguments from context and apply implicit functions through MLPs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a detailed mechanistic interpretation of factual recall in transformers, introducing a method to decompose MLP outputs and identifying a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer.
papers.conclusion: The paper outlines a pipeline for factual recall in transformers, proposes a novel analytic method for MLPs, and identifies a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism that can be mitigated to improve factual recall confidence.
papers.key_findings:
Task-specific attention heads extract topic tokens and pass them to subsequent MLPs.
MLPs act as activations that amplify or erase individual attention head outputs in the residual stream.
Deep MLPs apply implicit functions by adding a task-aware component that redirects the residual stream towards the correct answer.
A universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer suppresses correct predictions, which can be mitigated using the proposed interpretation.
These mechanisms are consistent across models (GPT-2, OPT, Llama-2), tasks (country-capital, product-developer), and few-shot settings.
papers.limitation:
The paper does not explore how the model constructs task semantics within its shallow layers.
The origins of the identified mechanisms (e.g., why MLPs redirect the residual stream) need further research.
The proposed analysis method for decomposing MLP outputs requires preliminary human reasoning and is not fully automated.
future_direction: Exploring how task semantics are constructed in shallow layers through collaborative circuit paths.
Investigating the origins of the mechanisms, such as why MLP outputs are structured as y-x.
Developing more automated interpretation techniques for MLPs.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we delve into several mechanisms employed by Transformer-based language models (LLMs) for factual recall tasks. We outline a pipeline consisting of three major steps: (1) Given a prompt ``The capital of France is,'' task-specific attention heads extract the topic token, such as ``France,'' from the context and pass it to subsequent MLPs. (2) As attention heads' outputs are aggregated with equal weight and added to the residual stream, the subsequent MLP acts as an ``activation,'' which either erases or amplifies the information originating from individual heads. As a result, the topic token ``France'' stands out in the residual stream. (3) A deep MLP takes ``France'' and generates a component that redirects the residual stream towards the direction of the correct answer, i.e., ``Paris.'' This procedure is akin to applying an implicit function such as ``get\_capital($X$),'' and the argument $X$ is the topic token information passed by attention heads. To achieve the above quantitative and qualitative analysis for MLPs, we proposed a novel analytic method aimed at decomposing the outputs of the MLP into components understandable by humans. Additionally, we observed a universal anti-overconfidence mechanism in the final layer of models, which suppresses correct predictions. We mitigate this suppression by leveraging our interpretation to improve factual recall confidence. The above interpretations are evaluated across diverse tasks spanning various domains of factual knowledge, using various language models from the GPT-2 families, 1.3B OPT, up to 7B Llama-2, and in both zero- and few-shot setups.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enhances performance of large language models, but questions remain about whether these reasoning traces faithfully reflect the internal processes of the model. We present the first comprehensive study of CoT faithfulness in large vision-language models (LVLMs), investigating how both text-based and previously unexplored image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation. Our work introduces a novel, fine-grained evaluation pipeline for categorizing bias articulation patterns, enabling significantly more precise analysis of CoT reasoning than previous methods. This framework reveals critical distinctions in how models process and respond to different types of biases, providing new insights into LVLM CoT faithfulness. Our findings reveal that subtle image-based biases are rarely articulated compared to explicit text-based ones, even in models specialized for reasoning. Additionally, many models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon we term ``inconsistent'' reasoning - correctly reasoning before abruptly changing answers, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning from unfaithful CoTs. We then apply the same evaluation pipeline to revisit CoT faithfulness in LLMs across various levels of implicit cues. Our findings reveal that current language-only reasoning models continue to struggle with articulating cues that are not overtly stated.

papers.title: Inferring Functionality of Attention Heads from their Parameters
papers.research_question: How to infer the functionality of attention heads in LLMs from their parameters without model training or inference, and to map how strongly heads implement predefined operations or to infer salient operations of a given head.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MAPS, a framework to infer attention head functionality directly from parameters, enabling mapping of predefined operations across heads and automatic characterization of salient operations.
papers.conclusion: Introduces MAPS, an efficient framework for inferring attention heads’ functionality from their parameters, and showcases its utility in systematically mapping functionality across the model and automatically characterizing salient operations of a given head.
papers.key_findings:
MAPS estimations correlate with head outputs during inference and are causally linked to model predictions.
MAPS reveals attention heads of certain operations that were overlooked in previous studies.
MAPS provides insights on function universality and architecture biases in LLMs.
Automatic pipeline produces plausible operation descriptions for most heads, as assessed by human judgment.
Heads often implement multiple relations, and smaller models tend to encode more relations per head.
papers.limitation: The automatic description pipeline sometimes hallucinates patterns not present in the mappings.
future_direction: Improve the automatic description pipeline to reduce hallucinations by using confidence aggregation, intrinsic classifiers, or NLI models.
papers.abstract: Attention heads are one of the building blocks of large language models (LLMs). Prior work on investigating their operation mostly focused on analyzing their behavior during inference for specific circuits or tasks. In this work, we seek a comprehensive mapping of the operations they implement in a model. We propose MAPS (Mapping Attention head ParameterS), an efficient framework that infers the functionality of attention heads from their parameters, without any model training or inference. We showcase the utility of MAPS for answering two types of questions: (a) given a predefined operation, mapping how strongly heads across the model implement it, and (b) given an attention head, inferring its salient functionality. Evaluating MAPS on 20 operations across 6 popular LLMs shows its estimations correlate with the head's outputs during inference and are causally linked to the model's predictions. Moreover, its mappings reveal attention heads of certain operations that were overlooked in previous studies, and valuable insights on function universality and architecture biases in LLMs. Next, we present an automatic pipeline and analysis that leverage MAPS to characterize the salient operations of a given head. Our pipeline produces plausible operation descriptions for most heads, as assessed by human judgment, while revealing diverse operations.

papers.title: Language Models Understand Us, Poorly
papers.research_question: What does it mean for language models to understand human language, and do current and future models achieve such understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that internal representations are sufficient for language understanding, critiques the Scaling Paradigm, and advocates for probing model internals to advance the science of understanding.
papers.conclusion: Current language models have limited understanding due to under-specified data, and scaling alone may not suffice without focusing on internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Understanding-as-representation is sufficient for language understanding, while as-reliability is necessary but not sufficient.
Current language models are limited by under-specification of meaning in their training data.
The Scaling Paradigm may be computationally infeasible for achieving human-like understanding.
Probing model internals is essential to advance the science of understanding.
Adding more modalities and human language aspects is needed for better models.
papers.limitation: The paper presents only one perspective and may not fully cover diverse fields or be ultimately correct.
future_direction: Probe model internals
Add more of human language such as intersubjective, multi-agent environments
Measure what models can learn
papers.abstract: Some claim language models understand us. Others won’t hear it. To clarify, I investigate three views of human language understanding: as-mapping, as-reliability and as-representation. I argue that while behavioral reliability is necessary for understanding, internal representations are sufficient; they climb the right hill. I review state-of-the-art language and multi-modal models: they are pragmatically challenged by under-specification of form. I question the Scaling Paradigm: limits on resources may prohibit scaled-up models from approaching understanding. Last, I describe how as-representation advances a science of understanding. We need work which probes model internals, adds more of human language, and measures what models can learn.

papers.title: Do Natural Language Descriptions of Model Activations Convey Privileged Information?
papers.research_question: Do natural language descriptions of model activations (verbalization) provide privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, or do they mainly convey input information and the verbalizer's own knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that existing verbalization methods often do not convey privileged knowledge about the target model's internals, but instead reflect input information or the verbalizer's own knowledge, highlighting the need for better benchmarks and controls.
papers.conclusion: The results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
For feature extraction datasets, a zero-shot baseline achieves high accuracy without access to activations, suggesting privileged knowledge may not be necessary for verbalization to succeed.
Prediction on reconstructed text (via inversion) matches verbalization performance, indicating tasks may elicit input text information rather than privileged knowledge.
Verbalizers often rely on their own world knowledge, especially when there is a mismatch between target and verbalizer knowledge, as shown in PersonaQA experiments.
Verbalization is sensitive to prompt phrasing, complicating interpretation of verbalizer outputs.
future_direction: Developing better benchmarks and experimental controls to assess verbalization methods.
papers.abstract: Recent interpretability methods have proposed to translate LLM internal representations into natural language descriptions using a second verbalizer LLM. This is intended to illuminate how the target model represents and operates on inputs. But do such activation verbalization approaches actually provide privileged knowledge about the internal workings of the target model, or do they merely convey information about its inputs? We critically evaluate popular verbalization methods across datasets used in prior work and find that they can succeed at benchmarks without any access to target model internals, suggesting that these datasets may not be ideal for evaluating verbalization methods. We then run controlled experiments which reveal that verbalizations often reflect the parametric knowledge of the verbalizer LLM which generated them, rather than the knowledge of the target LLM whose activations are decoded. Taken together, our results indicate a need for targeted benchmarks and experimental controls to rigorously assess whether verbalization methods provide meaningful insights into the operations of LLMs.

papers.title: Information Anxiety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of entity popularity on the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs, and do queries about popular entities cause ambiguity or confusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'information anxiety', a phenomenon where LLMs exhibit internal strains when processing highly popular queries, leading to rapid convergence of probability distributions but poor attention and inconsistent fact retrieval across lexical variations.
papers.conclusion: Information anxiety reveals vulnerabilities in LLMs' processing of prevalent information, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation and better pretraining data scrutiny.
papers.key_findings:
For highly popular questions, the predicted probability distribution converges earlier to the target distribution.
LLMs pay lower attention to constraint tokens in popular queries, indicating poor engagement with query details.
Retrieved facts across lexical variations become more dissimilar as query popularity increases, showing sensitivity to phrasing.
LLMs struggle to segregate facts from distinct relations for popular subjects, leading to higher inter-relation similarity.
Despite internal inconsistencies, LLMs remain confident in predictions for popular queries, as shown by high probability scores.
papers.limitation:
Entity and popularity formatted datasets like PopQA are hard to curate.
Developing better proxies for entity popularity in pretraining data is non-trivial.
Challenges in tracking and standardizing pretraining data quality due to volume and closed-source nature.
future_direction: Reducing sensitivity to lexical variations in knowledge queries.
Reducing popularity-dependent strains in internal mechanisms of LLMs.
Exploring alternative proxies for entity popularity in pretraining corpora.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance as knowledge repositories, enabling models to understand user queries and generate accurate and context-aware responses. Extensive evaluation setups have corroborated the positive correlation between the retrieval capability of LLMs and the frequency of entities in their pretraining corpus. We take the investigation further by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs. Our work focuses on three critical dimensions - the impact of entity popularity, the models' sensitivity to lexical variations in query formulation, and the progression of hidden state representations across LLM layers. Our preliminary findings reveal that popular questions facilitate early convergence of internal states toward the correct answer. However, as the popularity of a query increases, retrieved attributes across lexical variations become increasingly dissimilar and less accurate. Interestingly, we find that LLMs struggle to disentangle facts, grounded in distinct relations, from their parametric memory when dealing with highly popular subjects. Through a case study, we explore these latent strains within LLMs when processing highly popular queries, a phenomenon we term information anxiety. The emergence of information anxiety in LLMs underscores the adversarial injection in the form of linguistic variations and calls for a more holistic evaluation of frequently occurring entities.

papers.title: No Answer Needed: Predicting LLM Answer Accuracy from Question-Only Linear Probes
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that a simple linear probe on residual stream activations can predict an LLM's forthcoming answer correctness, revealing a linearly separable 'factual correctness' signal that generalizes across knowledge domains but fails for mathematical reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The analysis advances understanding of how LLMs encode self-assessment, providing evidence for a general 'Factual Correctness' direction while highlighting the structural distinctness of reasoning capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
A correctness signal is linearly separable in the activation space and generalizes from trivia questions to other factual knowledge datasets.
The correctness direction fails to generalize to mathematical reasoning tasks (GSM8K), indicating a structural misalignment between factual and arithmetic correctness.
Linear separability of correctness is low in early layers and saturates at intermediate transformer layers.
For models that answer 'I don't know', doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, suggesting the same direction captures implicit confidence.
The in-advance correctness signal is strongest and most consistent for the largest model tested (Llama 3.3 70B).
papers.limitation: The learned correctness direction does not generalize to arithmetic-reasoning tasks (GSM8K).
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) anticipate when they will answer correctly? To study this, we extract activations after a question is read but before any tokens are generated, and train linear probes to predict whether the model's forthcoming answer will be correct. Across three open-source model families ranging from 7 to 70 billion parameters, projections on this "in-advance correctness direction" trained on generic trivia questions predict success in distribution and on diverse out-of-distribution knowledge datasets, indicating a deeper signal than dataset-specific spurious features, and outperforming black-box baselines and verbalised predicted confidence. Predictive power saturates in intermediate layers and, notably, generalisation falters on questions requiring mathematical reasoning. Moreover, for models responding "I don't know", doing so strongly correlates with the probe score, indicating that the same direction also captures confidence. By complementing previous results on truthfulness and other behaviours obtained with probes and sparse auto-encoders, our work contributes essential findings to elucidate LLM internals.

papers.title: Large Language Models Do NOT Really Know What They Don't Know
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs' internal states reflect truthfulness or merely the process of recalling parametric knowledge.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLMs' internal states encode the process of knowledge recall, not truthfulness, making hallucination detection challenging for associated hallucinations.
papers.conclusion: Hidden states encode whether models rely on their parametric knowledge rather than truthfulness, so detection methods succeed for unassociated hallucinations but struggle for associated hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Associated Hallucinations (AHs) and Factual Associations (FAs) share similar internal processes and representational geometries.
Existing hallucination detection methods struggle to distinguish AHs from FAs, performing near random guessing.
Unassociated Hallucinations (UHs) are more separable in representation space and can be reliably detected.
Refusal tuning is less effective for AHs due to representational overlap with FAs, while it works better for UHs.
Subject popularity in pre-training data correlates with the prevalence of AHs and FAs, but not with UHs.
papers.limitation:
Focus on factual knowledge, not long-form or open-ended generation tasks
Lack of analysis on prompt-based hallucination detection approaches
Applicability limited to open-source LLMs, not black-box or large reasoning models
future_direction: Future evaluations should report detection performance separately for Associated Hallucinations and Unassociated Hallucinations.
Integrate LLMs with external feedback mechanisms, such as fact-checking modules or retrieval-based verifiers.
Prioritize improving detection of Associated Hallucinations due to their higher risk in practical deployments.
papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that large language models (LLMs) encode factuality signals in their internal representations, such as hidden states, attention weights, or token probabilities, implying that LLMs may "know what they don't know". However, LLMs can also produce factual errors by relying on shortcuts or spurious associations. These error are driven by the same training objective that encourage correct predictions, raising the question of whether internal computations can reliably distinguish between factual and hallucinated outputs. In this work, we conduct a mechanistic analysis of how LLMs internally process factual queries by comparing two types of hallucinations based on their reliance on subject information. We find that when hallucinations are associated with subject knowledge, LLMs employ the same internal recall process as for correct responses, leading to overlapping and indistinguishable hidden-state geometries. In contrast, hallucinations detached from subject knowledge produce distinct, clustered representations that make them detectable. These findings reveal a fundamental limitation: LLMs do not encode truthfulness in their internal states but only patterns of knowledge recall, demonstrating that "LLMs don't really know what they don't know".

papers.title: COMPASS: Context-Modulated PID Attention Steering System for Hallucination Mitigation
papers.research_question: How can contextual hallucinations in LLMs be reduced by dynamically steering attention to retrieved context during generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a lightweight framework that uses a PID controller and a Context Reliance Score to dynamically steer attention to context during generation, reducing hallucinations without retraining or multi-pass decoding.
papers.conclusion: Feedback-driven attention control is a feasible, low-overhead strategy for reducing hallucinations in LLMs, offering an interpretable alternative to opaque interventions.
papers.key_findings:
COMPASS reduces hallucination rates by 2.8–5.8% across benchmarks.
It decreases unsupported span density and improves context overlap metrics.
The method operates efficiently within a single decode stream without requiring model retraining.
Larger models (e.g., LLaMA-2-13B, Mistral-7B) benefit more from attention modulation, likely due to richer redundancy and head-level structure.
The framework provides an interpretable mapping between internal attention signals and model behavior.
papers.limitation:
Head-importance estimation may under-perform in extremely long-context or multi-turn settings where risk accrues gradually without strong local cues.
Gating decisions are made per step without global discourse awareness, so suppression of longer narrative drifts is limited.
Sensitivity to controller hyperparameters (EMA smoothing, hysteresis, PID gains, log-space slew limit and cap) can cause oscillatory activation, unstable convergence, or oversuppression of useful heads.
Computing CRS features and per-layer top-K selection adds modest but non-negligible overhead that can impact latency on smaller GPUs or very long sequences.
future_direction: Integration of richer detector signals that capture semantic coherence.
Formalizing stability guarantees for PID-controlled attention modulation.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often generate fluent but factually incorrect statements despite having access to relevant evidence, a failure mode rooted in how they allocate attention between contextual and parametric knowledge. Understanding and steering this internal behavior is key both for trustworthy deployment and for scientific interpretability of model mechanisms. We introduce COMPASS (Context-Modulated PID Attention Steering System), a lightweight, interpretable control framework that embeds a model-based feedback loop directly within decoding. COMPASS quantifies context reliance via a transparent metric, the Context Reliance Score (CRS), which serves as an online probe of how attention heads ground generation in evidence. Using this interpretable signal, a PID controller dynamically modulates attention heads to maintain factual consistency without retraining or multi-pass decoding. Across benchmarks (HotpotQA, XSum, HaluEval, RAGTruth), COMPASS consistently reduces contextual hallucination rates (2.8 to 5.8 percent absolute) while revealing how distinct attention heads contribute to evidence alignment. These results highlight feedback-driven interpretability as a pathway toward scientific understanding of LLM behavior.

papers.title: Localizing Lying in Llama: Understanding Instructed Dishonesty on True-False Questions Through Prompting, Probing, and Patching
papers.research_question: How can instructed dishonesty (lying) in a large language model be localized and understood using mechanistic interpretability methods?
papers.core_contribution: The paper localizes layers and attention heads responsible for instructed dishonesty in LLaMA-2-70b-chat, showing that causal interventions on just 46 heads can flip the model's behavior from lying to answering honestly.
papers.conclusion: The work contributes to understanding dishonesty in LLMs by localizing the behavior to specific layers and heads, enabling causal interventions that flip the model from lying to honesty, with the goal of informing methods to prevent such behavior.
papers.key_findings:
LLaMA-2-70b-chat can be instructed to lie on true/false questions, but this behavior is sensitive and requires careful prompt engineering, including the use of assistant response prefixes.
Linear probing and activation patching identify layers 19-23 as crucial for dishonest behavior, with representations between honest and liar prompts becoming anti-parallel after these layers.
Activation patching from an honest model into a lying model on layers 19-23 can significantly increase the liar's accuracy from 2% to 63%.
A subset of 46 attention heads within layers 19-23 (0.9% of all heads) is causally important for lying; patching these heads from honest to liar models flips the liar's behavior to be honest, and vice versa.
The intervention on the 46 heads generalizes robustly across different prompts and dataset splits (Cities, Inventions, Chemical Elements, Animals, Companies, Scientific Facts).
